claims.claim: HK022 integration separates the torS coding sequence from the IscR binding site that regulates its transcription.
claims.source: The integration site for bacteriophage HK022 is in the short intergenic region between the divergently transcribed genes torS and torT and separates the torS open reading frame from the IscR binding site that negatively regulates torS transcription (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: The text explicitly states this separation, and Figure 1A illustrates the genomic arrangement showing IscR binding site separated from torS by the prophage.

claims.claim: TorS and TorT together detect trimethylamine oxide (TMAO) in the periplasm and transduce this signal to phosphorylate the response regulator TorR.
claims.source: These genes produce a periplasmic binding protein and a sensor kinase, respectively, that together detect trimethylamine oxide (TMAO) in the periplasm and transduce this signal to the cytoplasm to phosphorylate the response regulator TorR.
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes the established function of TorS and TorT in TMAO detection and signal transduction.

claims.claim: Phosphorylated TorR activates transcription of the torCAD operon, which encodes TMAO reductase.
claims.source: Phosphorylated TorR then activates transcription of the torCAD operon, which encodes TMAO reductase (see Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: The text states this regulatory relationship and Figure 1A shows the pathway.

claims.claim: TMAO respiration enables E. coli to use TMAO as a respiratory electron acceptor.
claims.source: This pathway enables E. coli to use TMAO as a respiratory electron acceptor.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this metabolic function of the TMAO respiration pathway.

claims.claim: TMAO is widespread in the environment and particularly abundant in the tissues of many marine organisms.
claims.source: TMAO is widespread in the environment (Gibb and Hatton, 2004; Hatton and Gibb, 1999) and is particularly abundant in the tissues of many marine organisms (Eisert et al., 2005; Seibel and Walsh, 2002; Yancey et al., 1982).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies documenting TMAO distribution in the environment and marine organisms.

claims.claim: Animals can ingest significant amounts of TMAO from seafood-rich diets.
claims.source: Animals can ingest significant amounts of this compound from seafood-rich diets (Eisert et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing TMAO ingestion from seafood.

claims.claim: Humans and other mammals synthesize TMAO from trimethylamine (TMA) that is liberated from dietary precursors by the gut microbiota.
claims.source: In addition, humans and other mammals synthesize TMAO from trimethylamine (TMA) that is liberated from dietary precursors by the gut microbiota (Fennema et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites studies documenting TMAO synthesis from gut microbiota-derived TMA.

claims.claim: Circulating TMAO accumulates in urine and is excreted.
claims.source: Circulating TMAO accumulates in urine and is excreted (Hai et al., 2015; Velasquez et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing TMAO excretion in urine.

claims.claim: Aerobic torCAD expression occurs with high cell-to-cell variability in E. coli.
claims.source: We recently showed that aerobic expression of torCAD occurs with high cell-to-cell variability (Roggiani and Goulian, 2015), which can benefit the population by serving as a metabolic bet-hedging strategy in the face of a rapid decrease in oxygen availability (Carey et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites prior work demonstrating high variability in aerobic torCAD expression.

claims.claim: High cell-to-cell variability in aerobic torCAD expression can benefit the population by serving as a metabolic bet-hedging strategy during rapid oxygen depletion.
claims.source: We recently showed that aerobic expression of torCAD occurs with high cell-to-cell variability (Roggiani and Goulian, 2015), which can benefit the population by serving as a metabolic bet-hedging strategy in the face of a rapid decrease in oxygen availability (Carey et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites prior work showing the bet-hedging function of variable torCAD expression.

claims.claim: Highly variable torCAD expression is regulated by oxygen and is mediated by torS and torT.
claims.source: Highly variable torCAD expression is regulated by oxygen and is mediated by torS and torT, the genes that flank the HK022 integration site (Carey et al., 2018; Roggiani and Goulian, 2015).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites prior work showing oxygen regulation of torCAD variability through torS and torT.

claims.claim: The torS and torT genes are divergently transcribed but share a repressor binding site for the transcription factor IscR.
claims.source: The torS and torT genes are divergently transcribed but share a repressor binding site for the transcription factor IscR (Carey et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites prior work documenting the shared IscR binding site.

claims.claim: Under aerobic conditions, IscR repression leads to exceptionally low abundance of TorS and TorT protein and noisy transcription of the torCAD operon.
claims.source: Under aerobic conditions, IscR repression at this site leads to exceptionally low abundance of TorS and TorT protein and noisy transcription of the torCAD operon (Carey et al., 2018; Li et al., 2014; Taniguchi et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies documenting low TorS/TorT abundance and noisy torCAD transcription under aerobic conditions.

claims.claim: The HK022 integration site separates the torS coding sequence from the IscR binding site that regulates its transcription.
claims.source: Curiously, the HK022 integration site separates the torS coding sequence from the IscR binding site that regulates its transcription.
claims.evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this separation caused by HK022 integration.

claims.claim: The HK022 prophage eliminates aerobic torCAD transcription in E. coli K-12 carrying a fluorescent reporter.
claims.source: We grew this lysogenized reporter strain aerobically in the presence of TMAO and measured torCAD transcription in single cells by fluorescence microscopy. Transcription of torCAD was undetectable in the lysogen but was observed in the non-lysogen control strain (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: The text describes the experimental observation and Figure 1B shows the data demonstrating no aerobic torCAD expression in the lysogen.

claims.claim: The HK022 prophage does not eliminate anaerobic torCAD transcription in E. coli K-12.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, however, when we measured torCAD transcription in cells grown anaerobically in the presence of TMAO, we observed no difference between the lysogen and the non-lysogen (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: The text describes the experimental observation and Figure 1B shows similar anaerobic torCAD expression in lysogen and non-lysogen.

claims.claim: Cells without TorS cannot phosphorylate TorR and activate torCAD transcription.
claims.source: The simplest explanation for the loss of aerobic torCAD transcription in the lysogen is that the presence of the prophage destroys the torS promoter, as cells without TorS cannot phosphorylate TorR and activate torCAD transcription (Figure 1A) (Jourlin et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites prior work showing TorS is required for TorR phosphorylation and torCAD activation.

claims.claim: Only cells with a recent history of high torCAD expression are able to continue growth after oxygen depletion when TMAO is present and no other respiratory electron acceptors or fermentative substrates are available.
claims.source: We previously showed that high cell-to-cell variability in aerobic torCAD expression can function as a bet-hedging strategy that helps a population tolerate a rapid transition to anaerobiosis (Carey et al., 2018). Only cells with a recent history of high torCAD expression are able to continue growth after oxygen depletion when TMAO is present and no other respiratory electron acceptors or fermentative substrates are available.
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites prior work and describes the bet-hedging mechanism.

claims.claim: The HK022 lysogen is unable to employ the bet-hedging strategy and cannot grow through an aerobic-to-anaerobic transition under specific conditions.
claims.source: Because the HK022 lysogen does not express torCAD aerobically, we suspected that it would be unable to employ this bet-hedging strategy and would therefore be unable to grow through an aerobic-to-anaerobic transition under the conditions described above.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states the hypothesis based on the lack of aerobic torCAD expression in the lysogen.

claims.claim: Only the non-lysogen contains a subpopulation of cells that can grow substantially after oxygen depletion, and this subpopulation has high torCAD expression at the time of transition.
claims.source: The results of this experiment, shown in Figure 1C, D, indicate that only the non-lysogen contains a subpopulation of cells that can grow substantially after oxygen depletion and that this subpopulation has high torCAD expression at the time of transition.
claims.evidence: The text describes the results and Figures 1C and 1D show the growth data after oxygen depletion.

claims.claim: The HK022 prophage deactivates TMAO-dependent bet hedging on rapid oxygen depletion.
claims.source: From this we conclude that the HK022 prophage deactivates TMAO-dependent bet hedging on rapid oxygen depletion.
claims.evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: torS expression is substantially elevated in the HK022 lysogen compared to the non-lysogen.
claims.source: To investigate the effect of the prophage on torS transcription, we measured β-galactosidase activity produced from an operon fusion of lacZ to torS in the HK022 lysogen and non-lysogen, both with and without oxygen. We found that torS expression was substantially elevated in the HK022 lysogen (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The text describes the β-galactosidase assay results and Figure 2A shows elevated torS expression in the lysogen.

claims.claim: torT transcription shows no difference between the HK022 lysogen and non-lysogen.
claims.source: When we performed analogous experiments to measure torT transcription, we found no difference between the two strains (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The text describes the experimental results and Figure 2B shows similar torT expression in both strains.

claims.claim: The HK022 prophage shuts off aerobic torCAD transcription by increasing torS transcription while leaving torT transcription unchanged.
claims.source: These results suggest that the HK022 prophage shuts off aerobic torCAD transcription not by disrupting torS transcription but rather by increasing torS transcription while leaving torT transcription unchanged.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this interpretation based on the torS and torT expression data.

claims.claim: TorS molecules that are not bound to TorT are unable to detect TMAO and are in a state that dephosphorylates TorR.
claims.source: TorS molecules that are not bound to TorT are unable to detect TMAO and are in a state that dephosphorylates TorR (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites prior work (Ansaldi et al., 2001; Carey et al., 2018; Roggiani and Goulian, 2015) and shows this in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Cells with a large excess of TorS over TorT would strongly favor TorR dephosphorylation and not express torCAD.
claims.source: Therefore, cells with a large excess of TorS over TorT would strongly favor TorR dephosphorylation and not express torCAD (Ansaldi et al., 2001; Carey et al., 2018; Roggiani and Goulian, 2015).
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on cited prior work about TorS/TorT stoichiometry.

claims.claim: The HK022 lysogen shows elevated torS transcription in the absence of oxygen, yet torCAD is still expressed in these conditions.
claims.source: We note that the HK022 lysogen also shows elevated torS transcription in the absence of oxygen, and yet torCAD is still expressed in these conditions.
claims.evidence: The manuscript notes this observation from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Anaerobic TorT levels are sufficiently high for any additional TorS not to have much impact on TorR phosphorylation and torCAD expression.
claims.source: This suggests that anaerobic TorT levels are sufficiently high for any additional TorS not to have much impact on TorR phosphorylation and torCAD expression.
claims.evidence: The manuscript provides this interpretation to explain why elevated torS in the lysogen doesn't prevent anaerobic torCAD expression.

claims.claim: Overexpression of torT restores aerobic torCAD expression in an HK022 lysogen.
claims.source: To test this, we introduced a plasmid containing torT under control of a weakened trc promoter into the lysogen carrying the fluorescent torCAD transcriptional reporter and quantified torCAD expression (Figure 2C). The result of this experiment agrees with our prediction that the lysogen carrying the torT overexpression plasmid is able to express torCAD in the presence of oxygen.
claims.evidence: The text describes the experiment and Figure 2C shows restored aerobic torCAD expression with torT overexpression.

claims.claim: The HK022 phage encodes cis-acting element(s) near its attP site that affect torS transcription upon integration.
claims.source: We next wanted to probe the mechanism by which the HK022 prophage increases torS transcription. We hypothesized that the phage encodes some cis-acting element(s) near its attP site that, upon integration, affect torS transcription.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this hypothesis about the mechanism.

claims.claim: An outward-reading promoter within the HK022 prophage produces an mRNA transcript that reads through torS.
claims.source: A simple explanation would be an outward-reading promoter that produces an mRNA transcript originating from within the prophage and reading through torS.
claims.evidence: The manuscript proposes this mechanism as a hypothesis.

claims.claim: Insertion of a synthetic terminator at the boundary between bacterial and prophage sequence (attLHK022) results in very low torS expression during both aerobic and anaerobic growth.
claims.source: To test this explanation, we inserted a synthetic terminator construct—an Ω element (Prentki and Krisch, 1984)—at the boundary between bacterial and prophage sequence (attLHK022) (Figure 3A). We measured torS transcription in strains containing this terminator and found that torS expression was very low during both aerobic and anaerobic growth (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: The text describes the experiment and Figure 3B shows the low torS expression with the terminator insertion.

claims.claim: The mechanism by which the HK022 prophage activates torS expression is the production of torS transcripts that originate from within the prophage and are driven by a phage-encoded promoter.
claims.source: This result strongly suggests that the mechanism by which the HK022 prophage activates torS expression is the production of torS transcripts that originate from within the prophage and are driven by a phage-encoded promoter.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the terminator insertion experiment.

claims.claim: In vitro transcription from lysogen sequence produces a transcript different from transcripts produced from non-lysogen sequence.
claims.source: In vitro transcription from both plasmids produced transcripts, and the transcripts were different lengths when produced from lysogen sequence than when produced from non-lysogen sequence (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The text describes the in vitro transcription results and Figure 3C shows the different transcript lengths.

claims.claim: Transcripts of two distinct lengths are produced from the non-lysogen sequence, suggesting that there are two torS promoters when the prophage is absent.
claims.source: Interestingly, transcripts of two distinct lengths were produced from the non-lysogen sequence, suggesting that there are two torS promoters when the prophage is absent.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this interpretation based on the in vitro transcription data.

claims.claim: The transcript produced by the HK022 lysogen sequence maps to a single transcription start site located within the prophage.
claims.source: To confirm that the transcripts produced by in vitro transcription were truly torS transcripts and to map the transcription start sites associated with each of them, we performed primer extension assays (Figure 3D, E). The transcript produced by the HK022 lysogen sequence mapped to a single transcription start site located within the prophage (position indicated in Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: The text describes the primer extension results and Figures 3D and 3A show the transcription start site location.

claims.claim: The transcripts produced by the non-lysogen mapped to one transcription start site on the torS-proximal side of attBHK022 and one start site on the torS-distal side of attBHK022.
claims.source: The transcripts produced by the non-lysogen mapped to one transcription start site on the torS-proximal side of attBHK022 and one start site on the torS-distal side of attBHK022 (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: The text describes the primer extension results and Figure 3F shows the two transcription start sites.

claims.claim: The transcription start site for the shorter transcript (TSS2) is identical to a computationally predicted start site.
claims.source: The transcription start site for the shorter transcript (hereafter TSS2) is identical to a computationally predicted start site (Huerta and Collado-Vides, 2003), while the longer transcript (hereafter TSS1) has not previously been predicted or reported.
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a computational prediction that matches the experimentally determined TSS2.

claims.claim: TSS1 has not previously been predicted or reported.
claims.source: The transcription start site for the shorter transcript (hereafter TSS2) is identical to a computationally predicted start site (Huerta and Collado-Vides, 2003), while the longer transcript (hereafter TSS1) has not previously been predicted or reported.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states that TSS1 is a novel finding.

claims.claim: TSS2 is so close to attBHK022 that its promoter must be at least partially ablated after prophage integration.
claims.source: TSS2 is so close to attBHK022 that its promoter must be at least partially ablated after prophage integration; this likely explains why no TSS2 transcripts are observed in the lysogen.
claims.evidence: The manuscript provides this interpretation based on the proximity of TSS2 to the integration site.

claims.claim: TSS1 transcripts are likely absent in the lysogen because TSS1 lies on the far side of the attBHK022 site from the torS coding sequence.
claims.source: TSS1 transcripts, on the other hand, are likely absent in the lysogen because TSS1 lies on the far side of the attBHK022 site from the torS coding sequence; in the lysogen, the promoter and coding sequence are separated by the entire HK022 genome.
claims.evidence: The manuscript provides this interpretation based on the genomic arrangement after integration.

claims.claim: The only torS transcripts made in the HK022 lysogen are produced by a phage-encoded torS promoter and the int promoter is not required for prophage-regulated torS transcription.
claims.source: It appears, then, that the only torS transcripts made in the HK022 lysogen are produced by a phage-encoded torS promoter and that the int promoter is not required for prophage-regulated torS transcription.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the transcription start site mapping data.

claims.claim: TSS2 is within three base pairs of a predicted translation start site for torS and transcripts produced from TSS2 would not have room for a ribosome binding site.
claims.source: After identifying the transcription start sites, we realized that TSS2 is within three base pairs of a predicted translation start site for torS and that transcripts produced from TSS2 would not have room for a ribosome binding site.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this observation based on sequence analysis of the TSS2 region.

claims.claim: Only the lacZ fusion to the downstream ATG start codon produced β-galactosidase activity, suggesting that this codon is the primary or exclusive start codon for torS.
claims.source: To determine if either serves as a bona fide start codon, we constructed lacZ translational fusions to each and measured β-galactosidase activity. Only the lacZ fusion to the downstream ATG produced β-galactosidase activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The text describes the experiment and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 shows the β-galactosidase activity data.

claims.claim: Roughly 5% of sequenced E. coli genomes carry prophages integrated immediately upstream of torS.
claims.source: Roughly 5% of sequenced E. coli genomes carried prophages integrated immediately upstream of torS, and prophage-containing strains were not restricted to closely related E. coli phylogenetic groups (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from bioinformatic analysis of E. coli genomes.

claims.claim: Prophage-containing strains are not restricted to closely related E. coli phylogenetic groups.
claims.source: Roughly 5% of sequenced E. coli genomes carried prophages integrated immediately upstream of torS, and prophage-containing strains were not restricted to closely related E. coli phylogenetic groups (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: For every prophage identified, the prophage integrases were all more similar to HK022 integrase than to any other phage integrase.
claims.source: PHASTER indicated that the prophage integrases were all more similar to HK022 integrase than to any other phage integrase, and a multiple sequence alignment of the genomic region from torS to int revealed that, for every prophage, the attL site was in the same position relative to torS as attLHK022 (Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from PHASTER analysis and sequence alignment.

claims.claim: For every prophage identified, the attL site was in the same position relative to torS as attLHK022.
claims.source: PHASTER indicated that the prophage integrases were all more similar to HK022 integrase than to any other phage integrase, and a multiple sequence alignment of the genomic region from torS to int revealed that, for every prophage, the attL site was in the same position relative to torS as attLHK022 (Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from sequence alignment analysis.

claims.claim: Sequence conservation was high upstream of TSSHK022, suggesting conservation of the associated promoter.
claims.source: Sequence conservation was high upstream of TSSHK022, suggesting conservation of the associated promoter (despite there being no clearly identifiable −10 or −35 sequences).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports this observation from sequence alignment analysis.

claims.claim: torCAD expression in NRG 857C is much more similar to MG1655 HK022+ than to MG1655 without the prophage.
claims.source: When we measured torCAD transcription in NRG 857C during aerobic and anaerobic growth by fluorescence microscopy (Figure 4), we found that the pattern of expression was much more similar to MG1655 HK022+ than to MG1655 without the prophage (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: The text describes the experimental results and Figure 4 shows the torCAD expression pattern in NRG 857C.

claims.claim: In at least some wild E. coli strains there is prophage-mediated regulation of torCAD expression that is mechanistically similar to the HK022-mediated regulation seen in MG1655.
claims.source: This suggests that in at least some wild E. coli strains there is prophage-mediated regulation of torCAD expression that is mechanistically similar to the HK022-mediated regulation seen in MG1655.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the NRG 857C expression data.

claims.claim: Bacteriophage HK022 reconfigures the regulation of TMAO reductase expression in E. coli.
claims.source: In this work, we have shown that bacteriophage HK022 reconfigures the regulation of TMAO reductase expression in E. coli.
claims.evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this main conclusion.

claims.claim: By restricting torCAD expression to anaerobic conditions, HK022 converts oxygen-dependent regulation of the variance in torCAD expression into oxygen-dependent regulation of mean torCAD expression.
claims.source: By restricting torCAD expression to anaerobic conditions, HK022 converts oxygen-dependent regulation of the variance in torCAD expression (seen in non-lysogens) into oxygen-dependent regulation of mean torCAD expression (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion and Figure 5 illustrates the regulatory change.

claims.claim: HK022 reconfigures torCAD regulation by increasing expression of the regulatory protein TorS.
claims.source: HK022 reconfigures torCAD regulation by increasing expression of the regulatory protein TorS (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this mechanism and Figure 5 illustrates it.

claims.claim: The phage achieves increased TorS expression by replacing the native torS promoters with a promoter located within the prophage.
claims.source: The phage appears to achieve this by replacing the native torS promoters with a promoter located within the prophage.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the transcription start site mapping and terminator insertion experiments.

claims.claim: An outward-reading transcript originates from within the prophage and reads through torS.
claims.source: We mapped the transcription start site associated with this promoter to within the prophage and were able to abolish torS transcription initiated at this site by inserting a transcriptional terminator into the junction between the prophage and the E. coli chromosome (Figure 3). These results indicate that an outward-reading transcript originates from within the prophage and reads through torS.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: There must be a fitness cost to the expression of torCAD, or else its expression would not be regulated.
claims.source: We have argued previously that there must be a fitness cost to the expression of torCAD, or else its expression would not be regulated (Carey et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites prior work making this argument.

claims.claim: The HK022 prophage may prevent aerobic torCAD transcription to alleviate a fitness cost and thereby increase the rate of its own replication.
claims.source: The HK022 prophage may prevent aerobic torCAD transcription to alleviate a fitness cost and thereby increase the rate of its own replication.
claims.evidence: The manuscript proposes this as a speculative explanation for the prophage's effect.

claims.claim: Shutting down aerobic torCAD expression could be a useful strategy if phages like HK022 primarily lysogenize E. coli in environments where TMAO is present but rapid oxygen loss is unlikely to occur.
claims.source: If the primary function of aerobic torCAD expression is bet hedging on rapid oxygen depletion, shutting down aerobic expression could be a useful strategy if phages like HK022 primarily lysogenize E. coli in environments where TMAO is present but rapid oxygen loss is unlikely to occur.
claims.evidence: The manuscript proposes this as a speculative explanation.

claims.claim: The HK022 integration site is occupied by a prophage in roughly 5% of fully sequenced E. coli strains.
claims.source: The HK022 integration site is occupied by a prophage in roughly 5% of fully sequenced E. coli strains, and these prophages are found in E. coli of diverse origins and phylogenetic groups.
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from bioinformatic analysis.

claims.claim: Prophages occupying the HK022 integration site are found in E. coli of diverse origins and phylogenetic groups.
claims.source: The HK022 integration site is occupied by a prophage in roughly 5% of fully sequenced E. coli strains, and these prophages are found in E. coli of diverse origins and phylogenetic groups.
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from bioinformatic and phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: All of the prophages occupying the HK022 integration site have an outward-reading integrase gene as the final identifiable gene before torS.
claims.source: All of the prophages we identified occupying this site have, like HK022, an outward-reading integrase gene as the final identifiable gene before torS, and all share the general genomic architecture of phages belonging to the lambda supercluster (Grose and Casjens, 2014).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from sequence analysis.

claims.claim: All prophages occupying the HK022 integration site share the general genomic architecture of phages belonging to the lambda supercluster.
claims.source: All of the prophages we identified occupying this site have, like HK022, an outward-reading integrase gene as the final identifiable gene before torS, and all share the general genomic architecture of phages belonging to the lambda supercluster (Grose and Casjens, 2014).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from sequence analysis and cites a reference for lambda supercluster classification.

claims.claim: Two E. coli isolates, Nissle 1917 and HS, which do not have prophages integrated at attBHK022, have torCAD expression patterns that are like that of wild-type (uninfected) MG1655.
claims.source: In contrast, a previous study found that two other E. coli isolates, Nissle 1917 and HS, which do not have prophages integrated at attBHK022, have torCAD expression patterns that are like that of wild-type (uninfected) MG1655 (Roggiani and Goulian, 2015).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites prior work showing torCAD expression patterns in strains without prophages at attBHK022.

claims.claim: It may be a general capability of the phages that integrate between torS and torT to alter host regulation of torCAD expression.
claims.source: These observations suggest that it may be a general capability of the phages that integrate between torS and torT to alter host regulation of torCAD expression.
claims.evidence: The manuscript proposes this generalization based on the NRG 857C data and bioinformatic analysis.

claims.claim: The phenomenon described in this study, where a prophage rewires the regulation of a metabolic pathway by modulating the expression of a signaling gene, has not been reported before.
claims.source: To our knowledge, the phenomenon described in this study, where a prophage rewires the regulation of a metabolic pathway by modulating the expression of a signaling gene, has not been reported before and may exemplify a general class of mechanisms phages use to control host behavior.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this claim about the novelty of the mechanism.

claims.claim: The mechanism described may exemplify a general class of mechanisms phages use to control host behavior.
claims.source: To our knowledge, the phenomenon described in this study, where a prophage rewires the regulation of a metabolic pathway by modulating the expression of a signaling gene, has not been reported before and may exemplify a general class of mechanisms phages use to control host behavior.
claims.evidence: The manuscript proposes this as a broader implication of the findings.

claims.claim: Temperate bacteriophages can incorporate their genomes into their bacterial hosts, existing as prophages that refrain from killing the host cell until induced.
claims.source: Temperate bacteriophages are viruses that can incorporate their genomes into their bacterial hosts, existing there as prophages that refrain from killing the host cell until induced.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge about temperate phages.

claims.claim: Prophages can alter host phenotype through factors encoded in their genomes or by disrupting host genes as a result of integration.
claims.source: Prophages are largely quiescent, but they can alter host phenotype through factors encoded in their genomes (often virulence factors) or by disrupting host genes as a result of integration.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge about prophage effects on hosts.

claims.claim: A temperate phage that integrates in Escherichia coli reprograms host regulation of an anaerobic respiratory system, thereby inhibiting a bet hedging strategy.
claims.source: We show that a temperate phage that integrates in Escherichia coli reprograms host regulation of an anaerobic respiratory system, thereby inhibiting a bet hedging strategy.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this as a main finding in the abstract.

claims.claim: The phage exerts this effect by upregulating a host-encoded signal transduction protein through transcription initiated from a phage-encoded promoter.
claims.source: The phage exerts this effect by upregulating a host-encoded signal transduction protein through transcription initiated from a phage-encoded promoter.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this mechanism in the abstract.

claims.claim: This phenomenon occurs not only in a laboratory strain of E. coli, but also in a natural isolate that contains a prophage at this site.
claims.source: We further show that this phenomenon occurs not only in a laboratory strain of E. coli, but also in a natural isolate that contains a prophage at this site.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this finding in the abstract.

claims.claim: Lysogenic conversion can benefit the host by conferring abilities to produce toxins, resist antibiotics, increase virulence, and repel further phage infections.
claims.source: Prophage alteration of host phenotype, known as lysogenic conversion (Lederberg, 1955), can benefit the host by conferring abilities to produce toxins, resist antibiotics, increase virulence, and repel further phage infections (for recent reviews, see Argov et al., 2017; Bondy-Denomy and Davidson, 2014; Davies et al., 2016; Fortier and Sekulovic, 2013; Harrison and Brockhurst, 2017; Howard-Varona et al., 2017; Obeng et al., 2016; and Touchon et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites multiple reviews documenting these benefits of lysogenic conversion.

claims.claim: Lysogenic conversion traits are oftentimes encoded within prophage genetic elements called morons, which contain genes that are regulated by their own promoters and are not involved in the phage lytic cycle.
claims.source: Oftentimes these traits are encoded within prophage genetic elements called morons, which contain genes that are regulated by their own promoters and are not involved in the phage lytic cycle (Hendrix et al., 2000; Juhala et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites studies defining and characterizing morons.

claims.claim: Most phage genes have unknown function and no homology to any genes with known function.
claims.source: Although lysogenic conversion has been under study since its first description nearly 100 years ago (Frobisher and Brown, 1927), there are likely entire classes of phage-encoded proteins that impact host fitness in as-yet-undescribed ways, as most phage genes have unknown function and no homology to any genes with known function.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this as general knowledge about phage genomics.

claims.claim: Deleting all of the cryptic prophages in Escherichia coli BW25113 increased the strain's susceptibility to exogenous stresses and decreased its growth rate.
claims.source: One study found that deleting all of the cryptic prophages in Escherichia coli BW25113 increased the strain's susceptibility to exogenous stresses and decreased its growth rate through mechanisms yet to be understood (Wang et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing effects of prophage deletion.

claims.claim: The cI repressor of phage λ prevents expression of the λ lytic genes and also acts directly at the promoter of the metabolic gene pckA, repressing its expression and producing a slow growth phenotype in some conditions.
claims.source: Other studies have shown that host gene expression can be regulated by phage-encoded transcription factors, as in the case of the cI repressor of phage λ that is expressed during lysogeny. This protein prevents expression of the λ lytic genes but was also discovered to act directly at the promoter of the metabolic gene pckA (phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase), repressing its expression and producing a slow growth phenotype in some conditions (Chen et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing λ cI repressor effects on host metabolism.

claims.claim: Prophages can alter host gene expression by means of the position in the host genome where they integrate.
claims.source: Prophages can also alter host gene expression by means of the position in the host genome where they integrate (Bondy-Denomy and Davidson, 2014; McShan and Ferretti, 2007).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing position-dependent effects of prophage integration.

claims.claim: The Φ13 phage of Staphylococcus aureus integrates into the 5' end of the hlb gene, disabling β-toxin expression.
claims.source: For instance, the Φ13 phage of Staphylococcus aureus integrates into the 5' end of the hlb gene, disabling β-toxin expression (Coleman et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing gene disruption by prophage integration.

claims.claim: In some bacteria prophages act as switches that regulate host gene expression through controlled excision from interrupted genes, a phenomenon called active lysogeny.
claims.source: Disruption of host genes by prophage integration can be reversed by prophage excision, and in some bacteria prophages act as switches that regulate host gene expression through controlled excision from interrupted genes, a phenomenon called active lysogeny (Feiner et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a review defining and describing active lysogeny.

claims.claim: The Φ10403S prophage of Listeria monocytogenes integrates in and disrupts a gene required for efficient escape of the mammalian phagosome, and the prophage excises during infection to restore gene function.
claims.source: In Listeria monocytogenes, for example, the Φ10403S prophage integrates in and disrupts a gene that is required for efficient escape of the mammalian phagosome (Rabinovich et al., 2012). The prophage excises during infection, restoring gene function, but its bacterial lysis genes remain repressed. The excised phage later reintegrates back into the same gene without killing its host.
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing active lysogeny in L. monocytogenes.

claims.claim: In some cases, prophages involved in active lysogeny have lost the genes required for production of virions but still act as key regulators of cellular processes such as differentiation.
claims.source: In some cases, the prophages involved in active lysogeny have lost the genes required for production of virions but still act as key regulators of cellular processes such as differentiation (Feiner et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a review describing defective prophages in active lysogeny.

claims.claim: TMAO respiration allows E. coli to grow anaerobically, but it occurs even when oxygen is available.
claims.source: TMAO respiration allows E. coli to grow anaerobically, but it occurs even when oxygen is available (Ansaldi et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing aerobic TMAO respiration.

claims.claim: Aerobic TMAO respiration is surprising because of anaerobic respiration's relatively poor energy yield compared to aerobic respiration.
claims.source: This is surprising because of anaerobic respiration's relatively poor energy yield compared to aerobic respiration.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this as general knowledge about respiratory energetics.

claims.claim: NRG 857C belongs to phylogenetic group B2 and is distantly related to the laboratory strain MG1655 (which belongs to phylogenetic group A).
claims.source: This strain belongs to phylogenetic group B2 (Supplementary file 1) and is thus only distantly related to the laboratory strain MG1655 (which belongs to phylogenetic group A).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports phylogenetic group assignments from bioinformatic analysis.

claims.claim: The torCAD promoter sequences are identical between NRG 857C and MG1655.
claims.source: The torCAD promoter sequences are identical between NRG 857C and MG1655, enabling us to use the same PtorCAD-yfp reporter construct that we used in MG1655-derived strains to assess torCAD transcription in NRG 857C.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this sequence identity based on genomic analysis.

results.result: HK022 prophage integrates between torS and torT genes, physically separating the torS coding sequence from its IscR regulatory binding site.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, and C15 are well-supported by cited prior work (Yagil et al., 1989) and Figure 1A clearly illustrates the genomic arrangement. The integration site location and its consequence for regulatory architecture are established facts.

results.result: HK022 prophage eliminates aerobic torCAD expression while preserving anaerobic expression, thereby disabling the bet-hedging strategy that allows non-lysogen cells to grow after rapid oxygen depletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C17 are directly supported by fluorescence microscopy data in Figure 1B showing differential expression patterns. Claims C21-C22 are supported by time-lapse microscopy data in Figures 1C-D demonstrating growth differences after oxygen depletion. The experimental design includes appropriate controls.

results.result: The HK022 prophage increases torS transcription substantially while leaving torT transcription unchanged, explaining the shutdown of aerobic torCAD expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C24 are supported by β-galactosidase assays shown in Figures 2A-B with appropriate replication. Claim C25 logically follows from the data and established knowledge about TorS/TorT stoichiometry (C26-C27). The interpretation is consistent with the mechanistic model.

results.result: Overexpression of torT restores aerobic torCAD expression in HK022 lysogen, confirming that the imbalance in TorS/TorT ratio is responsible for the phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claim C30 is supported by fluorescence microscopy data in Figure 2C showing rescue of aerobic torCAD expression upon torT overexpression. This genetic complementation experiment provides strong support for the proposed mechanism involving TorS/TorT stoichiometry.

results.result: Insertion of a transcriptional terminator at the prophage-chromosome junction abolishes torS expression, demonstrating that torS transcripts originate from within the prophage and are driven by a phage-encoded promoter.
results.evaluation: Claim C33 is supported by β-galactosidase data in Figure 3B showing very low torS expression with terminator insertion. Claims C34 and C57 are well-supported conclusions from this critical experiment that directly tests the proposed mechanism. The terminator insertion provides strong evidence for read-through transcription from the prophage.

results.result: In vitro transcription and primer extension mapping reveal that the lysogen produces a single torS transcript from a prophage-encoded promoter (TSSHK022), while non-lysogens produce two transcripts from distinct promoters (TSS1 and TSS2), with TSS2 matching a computationally predicted site and TSS1 being novel.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C40 are supported by in vitro transcription data (Figure 3C) and primer extension assays (Figures 3D-F). The experimental approach is appropriate for mapping transcription start sites. The identification of TSS2 is validated by computational prediction, while TSS1 represents a novel finding. The data quality appears sufficient for the conclusions drawn.

results.result: The native torS promoters (TSS1 and TSS2) are functionally disrupted by prophage integration due to their positions relative to the integration site, with TSS2's promoter ablated and TSS1 separated from torS by the entire prophage genome.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43 are logical inferences well-supported by the transcription start site mapping data and genomic arrangement shown in Figures 3A and 3F. The spatial relationships between integration site and promoters provide a clear mechanistic explanation for why native promoters are non-functional in the lysogen.

results.result: The downstream ATG codon, not the upstream GTG codon, serves as the primary translation start site for torS, as demonstrated by translational lacZ fusions.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C45 are supported by β-galactosidase assays from translational fusions shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1. The experimental design directly tests which start codon is functional. This finding clarifies the torS translation initiation site and is important for understanding the regulatory architecture.

results.result: Bioinformatic analysis reveals that approximately 5% of sequenced E. coli genomes contain prophages at the HK022 integration site, distributed across diverse phylogenetic groups, with conserved integrase sequences, attL site positions, and promoter regions upstream of TSSHK022.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C50 are supported by systematic bioinformatic analysis using BLAST, PHASTER, and sequence alignment tools. The methodology is appropriate for genome-scale analysis. The findings demonstrate that prophage integration at this site is widespread and evolutionarily conserved, though the 5% frequency should be interpreted cautiously as it depends on the genome database composition.

results.result: The wild E. coli strain NRG 857C, which naturally carries a prophage at the HK022 integration site, exhibits torCAD expression patterns similar to HK022-infected MG1655, suggesting the mechanism is not unique to laboratory strains.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52 are supported by fluorescence microscopy data in Figure 4 showing similar expression patterns between NRG 857C and HK022-infected MG1655. The strain construction is well-documented with appropriate genetic controls to ensure the tor and isc loci were not replaced during reporter integration. This extends the findings beyond laboratory conditions.

results.result: HK022 prophage reconfigures torCAD regulation by replacing native torS promoters with a phage-encoded promoter, converting oxygen-dependent regulation of expression variance into oxygen-dependent regulation of mean expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 and C71-C72 represent the main conclusions synthesizing multiple experimental results. These are well-supported by the collective evidence from expression studies (Figures 1-2), transcription start site mapping (Figure 3), and terminator insertion experiments. The mechanistic model is internally consistent and explains all major observations.

results.result: Unbound TorS dephosphorylates TorR, and excess TorS over TorT prevents torCAD expression; however, anaerobic TorT levels are sufficiently high that additional TorS does not prevent torCAD expression under anaerobic conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C27 are supported by cited prior work establishing TorS/TorT stoichiometry effects. Claims C28-C29 are logical inferences explaining why the lysogen maintains anaerobic torCAD expression despite elevated torS. The interpretation is consistent with the data and mechanistic understanding.

results.result: All identified prophages at the HK022 integration site share conserved features including outward-reading integrase genes and lambda supercluster genomic architecture, suggesting a general capability to alter torCAD regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64 are supported by sequence analysis data. Claim C66 is a reasonable inference based on the NRG 857C data and bioinformatic analysis, though the authors appropriately note that variation in prophage sequences and host genomes may affect this generalization. The conclusion is appropriately cautious.

results.result: The mechanism whereby a prophage rewires metabolic pathway regulation by modulating signaling gene expression represents a novel phenomenon that may exemplify a general class of phage-host control mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claim C67 asserts novelty based on the authors' knowledge, but comprehensive literature searches are difficult to verify. Claim C68 is speculative about broader implications. While the specific mechanism described is well-characterized, the claims about novelty and generalizability require more extensive comparative analysis across phage-host systems.

results.result: The TMAO respiration pathway in E. coli involves TorS/TorT detection of TMAO, TorR phosphorylation, and torCAD operon activation; aerobic expression is highly variable due to IscR repression and serves as a bet-hedging strategy for rapid oxygen depletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5 and C18 describe established knowledge about the TMAO pathway supported by appropriate citations. Claims C10-C14 and C19 cite the authors' prior work establishing the bet-hedging mechanism. These provide essential background context and are well-supported by the cited literature.

results.result: The fitness cost of torCAD expression may explain why HK022 prevents aerobic expression, potentially benefiting phage replication in environments where TMAO is present but rapid oxygen depletion is unlikely.
results.evaluation: Claim C58 cites prior work arguing for fitness costs. Claims C59-C60 are explicitly speculative explanations for the adaptive significance of the prophage's effect. While plausible, these hypotheses lack direct experimental support and would require fitness measurements and ecological studies to validate.

results.result: TMAO is environmentally widespread, particularly in marine organisms, can be ingested from diet or synthesized from gut microbiota-derived TMA, and is excreted in urine; aerobic TMAO respiration occurs despite poor energy yield compared to aerobic respiration.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C9 are supported by multiple appropriate citations documenting TMAO distribution and metabolism. Claims C84-C85 cite prior work and state general knowledge about respiratory energetics. These provide important biological context for understanding the significance of torCAD regulation.

results.result: Temperate phages can alter host phenotypes through lysogenic conversion via phage-encoded factors (often in morons), disruption of host genes, or position-dependent integration effects; examples include toxin production, antibiotic resistance, metabolic changes, and active lysogeny.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C83 provide comprehensive background on lysogenic conversion supported by extensive appropriate citations. These establish the broader context of phage-host interactions and demonstrate that the authors' work fits within an established field while potentially representing a novel mechanism.

results.result: Prophages occupy the HK022 integration site in ~5% of E. coli strains across diverse phylogenetic groups; strains without prophages (Nissle 1917, HS) show expression patterns like wild-type MG1655; NRG 857C is phylogenetically distant from MG1655 but has identical torCAD promoter sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 are supported by bioinformatic analysis. Claim C65 appropriately cites prior work. Claims C87-C88 are supported by phylogenetic analysis and sequence comparison. These findings establish the distribution and conservation of relevant genetic elements across E. coli diversity.

results.result: The authors hypothesized that HK022 encodes cis-acting elements near attP that affect torS transcription, potentially through an outward-reading promoter producing transcripts that read through torS.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32 represent hypotheses that were subsequently tested and confirmed by the terminator insertion and transcription mapping experiments. These hypotheses were reasonable based on the initial observations and led to productive experimental designs.
